newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram proposes cotton excise change.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram proposes cotton excise change.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Tuesday proposed raising a price threshold above which processors pay an excise duty on cotton fabrics.
In a brief statement to the lower house of parliament, Chidambaram said he proposed raising the price level above which processors would pay a higher excise tax.

In the 1996/97 (April-March) budget which Chidambaram presented to parliament in July, he proposed requiring independent processors to pay a basic excise duty of five percent for cotton fabrics costing up to 25 rupees per square metre. The rate would be 10 percent on all other fabrics.
On Tuesday Chidambaram said he was proposing raising the "cutoff point" for cotton fabrics to 30 rupees per square metre from 25 rupees.

"Cotton fabrics up to a value of 30 rupees per square metre will be charged basic excise duty at the rate of five percent, and the additional excise duty in lieu of sales tax also at the rate of five percent," he said.

Chidambaram said that under the proposed change, cotton fabrics valued at more than 30 rupees per square metre would draw basic excise duty of 12 percent and an additional excise duty of eight percent.
All other fabrics would be subject to basic excise duty at the rate of 12 percent as well as the additional excise duty in lieu of sales tax at the rate of eight percent, he said.
Chidambaram said he would retain the modified value-added tax (MODVAT) credit for cotton fabrics at the rate of 50 percent of duty paid.
However, he proposed increasing the percentage to 70 percent in the case of all other fabrics.
The finance minister said the changes would take effect on Wednesday.

When he presented the budget in July, Chidambaram said the introduction of the MODVAT credit scheme for textile fabrics would bring textiles into the mainstream of a tax system which he said tends to reduce, if not eliminate, the cascading effect of input taxes.

"This would also enable the composite mills and the processing houses to modernise and to produce high quality fabrics which would have a positive impact on exports of textiles and garments," he said in a written statement released on Tuesday.
